Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Life’s Challenges

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

¿Por qué adorar a un Dios que permite el sufrimiento?

Comparte este artículo

Pregunta: “¿Por qué alabar a un Dios que permite cosas horribles, como que un niño sea violado?”

Probablemente no hay mayor violación que la de un niño. Es devastador para la víctima en muchos sentidos. Cuando se acepta, la rabia es apropiada. No hay explicación para tales acciones.

Sin embargo, no es culpa de Dios que las personas elijan tomar lo bueno que Él ha creado y corromperlo. No es Su culpa que los padres abusen de sus hijas o que las madres agredan verbalmente a sus hijos.

Los seres humanos somos bastante libres de hacer lo que queramos.

¿Cómo nos deberíamos sentir sobre el hecho de que Dios no impida que otras personas nos hagan el mal?

¿Cómo nos deberíamos sentir sobre el hecho de que Dios no nos impida hacer el mal a otras personas?

Podríamos desear que Dios estableciera una serie de límites, más allá de los cuales la gente sería castigada. Podríamos sugerir que Dios matara a cualquier hombre que abusara de un niño.

Entonces ¿qué hay de los productores de porno infantil que podrían haber ayudado a motivar al hombre a abusar del niño? ¿Estaría bien si tal vez Dios los matara también?

Bien, ¿qué debería hacer Dios con, digamos, las personas que son verbalmente agredidas? Las palabras también pueden herir profundamente. Parece bastante evidente que podemos hacer lo que elegimos hacer. Y no veo cómo podemos enojarnos con Dios por dejarnos hacer eso.

¿No nos ha revelado Dios lo que es mejor para nuestras vidas?

¿No es cierto que si todo el mundo siguiera los 10 mandamientos, ningún niño sería violado o abusado?

¿No es cierto que si todo el mundo siguiera los 10 mandamientos, nunca se robaría nada, nunca se traicionaría a un cónyuge, no se asesinaría a ningún hijo o hija?

A child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance. Atheism cannot supply this reassurance. It does not reduce suffering one bit; it just removes hope. In an atheistic universe there is no ultimate accountability or justice. Evil people will get away with what they’ve done.

But in the Christian worldview, God has done something about evil in the person of Jesus Christ. He did not just stay in heaven and say, “OK you suckers, suffer!” He has given us a clue, a deposit, a down payment that he does have good reasons for allowing evil and that he does have a greater good in store. He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form. And what did he do when he was here? HE SUFFERED!

Jesus endured a suffering beyond all comprehension. He took upon himself and bore the just punishment of the sins of the whole world! For all the evil that everyone of us from the beginning of our species has perpetrated, he paid the just penalty. None of us can comprehend that suffering. Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve. And why? Because he loves us. It is like he is saying, “I know you don’t understand why I permit every evil. It’s not possible for you to understand yet. But just to show you that you can trust me, I’m going to suffer with you.”

I hear how much weight is behind this question — it's not just philosophical for you, it's raw. And I want to be honest: I don't think there's an answer that makes a child's suffering feel okay. Anyone who tries to hand you a tidy explanation that erases the horror of it is dodging something real. So let me try to share what these sources actually say, without pretending it resolves the pain.

**Freedom and its cost.** EveryStudent puts it starkly: humans are "pretty much free to do as we choose," and God "does not interfere with anyone's choices." The suggestion is that a world where love and moral choice are real requires a world where cruelty is also genuinely possible — God could have made a world of puppets who can't hurt each other, but that's not the kind of freedom or relationship he seems to have built us for ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

**This isn't the whole story, and suffering isn't the "final word."** Cru's piece frames it this way: "The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life." It points to a larger arc — how suffering entered the world, and God's plan to end it — rather than suffering being evidence God doesn't care ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html)).

**Some suffering is just built into a physical world.** One source (Sightline Ministry) points to the story of the man born blind — Jesus was asked whose sin caused it, and he said neither. Some suffering comes from others' choices, some from a physical world governed by consistent laws (gravity, disease, accidents) that God doesn't selectively suspend even for the innocent: "God doesn't take those laws away for good people" ([Sightline Ministry](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).

**And here's the part I think matters most for your question**: thelife.com argues that Christianity's answer isn't primarily an argument — it's that God didn't stay distant from this. "He has given us a clue... that he does have good reasons for allowing evil... He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form. And what did he do when he was here? HE SUFFERED!" The claim is that Jesus entered into suffering rather than explaining it away from a safe distance — and that "a child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance" ([thelife](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).

I want to be straight with you: none of this is a logical proof that closes the case. It's more like — God's response to the problem of suffering isn't an argument, it's a person who suffered too. Whether that lands as comfort or as still not enough is something only you can weigh. Can I ask — is this question coming from something happening around you right now, or more from watching the world and struggling with it?

happened after a game of chess. “Daddy, do you know where you’ll spend eternity when you die?” I asked him. “Well, I hope I’ll go to heaven, baby,” he replied. “Can I share with you how you can be sure?”

He said yes, and I explained how eternal security centered on him having a personal relationship with God through the forgiveness of sin Jesus offers.

“Are you ready to invite Jesus into your life and begin a personal relationship with God?”

“Yes, I am,” he said. Then he prayed and received Christ. “Mel, I feel so clean, I just feel so clean,” he said. I was in awe and amazed at what God had done — in my dad’s life and in mine.

But then death came as it often does — unexpected, unwanted and unrelenting. He passed away in his sleep a year after that prayer, at the young age of 56.

His heart just stopped beating. I was 26, and when he died, it felt like my heart stopped beating too. With his death went all the things I didn’t get a chance to do with him, to say to him.

I miss the conversations that never happened. I would have loved to talk with him about music. He was a musician at heart. He played several instruments and sang. I believe my deep love for funk bands, soul and R&B comes directly from him.

Grieving my dad continues more than a decade later. The first year was the hardest. But God held me together in the moments when I wanted to fall apart. Psalm 68:3-5 reminds me of His commitment to those who’ve lost their fathers this side of heaven.

God comforts those who grieve and mourn. He knows loss and deep grief well. He leads us to resources to help us when we lose those we love, like Journeying through Grief or the book “Experiencing Grief” by H. Norman Wright.

“We are of good courage, I say, and prefer rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 5:8

When I found out my friend’s brother had passed away, also a friend of mine, I was in shock. I couldn’t really believe it. He was so young. Because I couldn’t wrap my mind around it, I also questioned Why him? Why not someone else I didn’t know? Why not somebody old and ready to go? I thought those terrible things, thinking selfishly instead of selflessly. Where did he go? I wondered. Was he sitting around, unable to wake up, waiting for the resurrection?

I had to ask someone who knew, someone who could direct me to the Scriptures. It was there that I realized that no, indeed, he wasn’t just sitting around waiting for Christ to come. In fact, he was already in Heaven. That was made clear when Jesus told the thief on the cross that he would be with Him that very day in paradise. Scripture pointed to a God who immediately accepted His children upon their death. I was comforted. What I had once seen as a curse to those on earth, perhaps even to him because he had lost out on a long life, I now saw to be a mercy, to be a blessing. To be able to stand face to face with God and enjoy in eternal delights, to be able to see the angels, to be free from sin, death, and sorrow, was to be blessed. I longed to see it for myself, realizing he had gotten to see something I had always wanted to see but still had to wait for it as I dwelt on earth. We who were grieving were the only ones suffering, not him.

Friend, are you grieving right now? Take comfort in the joy of knowing that your saved loved one is reveling in the splendor of the Lord, in His very presence, not in any type of pain or sorrow, just pure joy.

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.
sources.title: The Life :: Dealing With the Fear of Death

Before her death, my mother became convinced that the Spirit of Christ was in her, that she belonged to him, and that she would live forever with him. The very thought of what awaited her filled her with great joy.

I was there when she died — praying for her, singing Bible verses to her, and holding her hand as she let out one last soft breath. The palliative care nurse who was with me turned to me and said: “I have never seen anyone go so peacefully from this life to the next.”

In the hours leading up to that moment, my mother, in a coma, would often lift her arms up to heaven, a peaceful smile on her face. Was she seeing Jesus welcoming her into his presence forever?

When Our Day Comes

One day, it will be our turn. Our friends will meet one another and say, “Have you heard about (our name)?”

My earnest prayer for you is that when someone blurts out, “No, what happened?”, the answer will be, “(Your name) went to be with Jesus forever.”

Would you like to put your trust in Jesus and begin to experience an eternal relationship with him right now? Why not tell him so? That's what prayer is: simply telling God what is on your heart and listening to his answer.

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.
sources.title: The Life :: Wrestling with God after my Father's Suicide

I'm really sorry about your dad. Losing a parent is painful enough, and carrying questions about his eternity on top of that grief is a heavy weight to hold. I want to be honest with you rather than guess, so let me look into what's grounded on this.First, I'm so sorry. A month is still so raw — please be gentle with yourself as you carry this.

I want to be honest with you: none of what I found gives a direct, clear teaching on the specific question of what happens to someone who never went to church or never made a profession of faith before dying. What these sources do speak to is what happens for those who do trust in Jesus — and a few honest wrestling with grief and unanswered questions, which might resonate with where you are.

A few things worth sharing:

- From **Cru** ("Forgiving My Dad Set Us Both Free," https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/life-and-relationships/holidays/forgiving-my-dad-set-us-both-free.html) — the author's father made a personal decision to receive Christ near the end of his life, even after not having that relationship for most of it. It's a reminder that these things aren't always tidy or "churchy" — some come to faith unexpectedly, in a conversation, in private.

- From **thelife.com** ("What Kind of Eternal Life Does Jesus Offer Us?", https://thelife.com/what-kind-of-eternal-life-does-jesus-offer-us) — the emphasis is on a person's trust in Jesus and relationship with him, not on church attendance itself, as what these writers describe as key to what comes after death.

- Also from **thelife.com** ("Wrestling with God after my Father's Suicide," https://thelife.com/after-my-fathers-suicide) — this writer describes very similar territory to yours: aching uncertainty about a father's relationship with God, guilt, unanswered questions, and still choosing to cling to God through the pain rather than having every answer.

I don't have a grounded source here that spells out God's judgment for someone who never heard the gospel or never had that conversation — so I won't pretend to know what these sources don't say. What I can say honestly is that not going to church isn't the same as never having had a private moment with God that only he was witness to. You may never know the full story of what happened in your dad's heart, and that unknowing is a hard thing to sit with.

Can I ask — was there any part of his life, however small, where you saw him reaching toward God, even if it never looked like "faith" in an obvious way? Sometimes those threads matter more than we realize.

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Can You Explain the Trinity?

The following clearly and briefly explains the Trinity … three gods or one?

By EveryStudent.com

Listen to article | Share this article

You and I live in a three-dimensional world. All physical objects have a certain height, width, and depth. One person can look like someone else, or behave like someone else, or even sound like someone else. But a person cannot actually be the same as another person. They are distinct individuals.

God, however, lives without the limitations of a three-dimensional universe. He is spirit. And he is infinitely more complex than we are.

That is why Jesus the Son can be different from the Father. And, yet the same.

The Bible clearly speaks of: God the Son, God the Father, and God the Holy Spirit. But emphasizes that there is only ONE God.

If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God.

Thus the term: "Tri" meaning three, and "Unity" meaning one, Tri+Unity = Trinity. It is a way of acknowledging what the Bible reveals to us about God, that God is yet three "Persons" who have the same essence of deity.

Some have tried to give human illustrations for the Trinity, such as H2O being water, ice and steam (all different forms, but all are H2O). Another illustration would be the sun. From it, we receive light, heat and radiation. Three distinct aspects, but only one sun.

No illustration is going to be perfect.

But from the very beginning, we see God as a Trinity. In the book of Genesis, the first book in the Bible, God says, "Let us make man in our image … male and female he created them."1 You see here a mixture of plural and singular pronouns.

When Moses asked God for his name, God replied, "I am" - eternally existing.

Jesus used the same phrase numerous times.

"I am the light of the world…"

"I am the bread of life…"

"I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

Yes, it does, because of the Trinity.

The Trinity is perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith. It asserts that there is one God who exists eternally in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. While many have tried to explain the mystery with analogies and metaphors — from a three-leaf clover to the states of matter to the colors of a traffic light — the truth is all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding.

But at the root of the doctrine of a trinitarian God are a few simple ideas. God is One, and He is above all. There is only one of Him in essence and character. But He is also relational — being three persons — and the Father, Son and Holy Spirit have loved, interacted with and rejoiced over each other for all of eternity. In Michael Reeves’ book “Delighting in the Trinity”, he delves into this theology, explaining that he believes this is where creation came from. An ever-giving God overflowed in love, truth and relationship, and from that came all that was good and free.

That's a really good question to ask — and it's not a sign that something's wrong with you for finding it puzzling. Christians themselves acknowledge it's genuinely mysterious.

Here's the key move that resolves the *apparent* contradiction: God is one in **essence**, but three in **person**. According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," these are two different categories, not the same claim twice. It would only be a contradiction if Christians said God is three in the *same way* he is one (source: [Cru, "Entender la Trinidad"](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

So concretely, the doctrine holds three things together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are **distinct persons** — not just three names or three roles for the same individual. Cru's article points out that since "the Father sent the Son into the world" (John 3:16) and the Father and Son together "sent the Holy Spirit into the world" (John 14:26; Acts 2:33), they can't simply be the same person wearing different masks (source: [Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief"](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).
2. Each person — Father, Son, and Spirit — is **fully God**. The Bible calls the Father God, calls Jesus God, and calls the Holy Spirit God (same Cru source).
3. Yet there is **only one God**, one essence, one "being" — not three beings or three gods.

EveryStudent.com puts it with a memorable bit of math: it's not 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1. "Tri" (three) + "unity" (one) = Trinity — God is three Persons sharing one essence of deity (source: [EveryStudent, "Can You Explain the Trinity?"](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

People have reached for analogies to make this less abstract — water existing as liquid, ice, and steam while remaining H2O, or the sun giving off light, heat, and radiation as three distinct effects of one sun (sources: [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html) and the German EveryStudent site, [Dreieinigkeit](https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html)). But it's worth being honest: every one of these analogies is admitted to fall short, because there's nothing else in creation that is both fully unified and fully personal in three distinct ways at once. As Cru's "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" article puts it, "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding."

So the short answer to "isn't this a contradiction?" — no, because "one" and "three" are answering different questions (essence vs. person), not the same question twice. But it remains a *mystery* in the proper sense: not irrational, but beyond full human comprehension.

What's prompting the question for you — is it more the logical puzzle, or are you wondering what difference it actually makes for how Christians relate to God?

One of the most important features of Christian faith is accepting that Jesus is God. Christians are in trouble, then, if Jesus never made such a claim of himself! Yet many have argued that this is exactly the case: Jesus never claimed to be God, they say, and his divinity is an invention of the Christian church. Is this true?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.

**The short answer: Jesus never says the exact English phrase "I am God."** But according to the sources I found, he made several statements that his listeners understood as claims to divinity — and those claims are recorded as his own direct words, not just later theological commentary.

Here are the clearest examples, drawn from **Sightline Ministry** (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god and https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false) and **Jesus Film Project** (https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts):

1. **"Before Abraham was born, I am!"** (John 8:58) — Jesus uses the same phrase God used to identify himself to Moses at the burning bush ("I AM," Exodus 3:14). According to Jesus Film Project, the crowd's reaction shows they understood this as a divine claim — they picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy.

2. **"I and the Father are one."** (John 10:30) — Sightline Ministry notes that a respected Greek scholar, A.T. Robertson, explains the Greek word "one" here points to unity in essence or nature, not just purpose. The Jewish leaders again responded by trying to stone him.

3. At his trial, the high priest asked Jesus directly, **"Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?"** Jesus answered, **"I am."** (Mark 14:61–62, as cited by Sightline Ministry). The high priest tore his robes and cried "Blasphemy!" — a reaction that only makes sense if Jesus's answer was understood as a claim to divine identity.

4. **"My Father is always working, and so am I."** (John 5:17) — Sightline Ministry points out that by saying "MY Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus was placing himself on equal footing with God in a way his Jewish audience couldn't misread — and John 5:18 records that this is exactly how they took it, wanting to kill him "because he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God."

So while Jesus doesn't use the literal sentence "I am God," his actual recorded words — especially "I am" (echoing God's name) and "I and the Father are one" — were taken by the people standing right there as unmistakable divine claims. That's not later interpretation layered on; it's how his own contemporaries reacted in the moment, according to these texts.

If you want, I can dig further into any one of these passages — like the context around John 8:58 or the trial scene in Mark — to see the fuller conversation around them.

“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:13-14).

Jesus lived a sinless life, and through His sacrifice, our account can be cleared of the debt against us. His death canceled the record of our debt. There is no longer a record against those who walked with Jesus. And the debt was paid so it no longer stood between us and God.

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!

That's a really common concern, and it's good that you're asking rather than just taking it at face value. The short answer, based on the sources I found: your uncle's concern makes sense on the surface, but scholars actually have strong tools to address it — and the evidence points the other way.

**Here's the key issue:** We don't have the *original* handwritten manuscripts of any biblical book — that's true of basically all ancient literature. But that doesn't mean we're lost. As Sightline Ministry explains, "we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts... there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (Sightline Ministry, "Has the Bible Been Altered Over the Centuries?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**The numbers matter here.** According to EveryStudent ("Jesus in Islam," https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html), there are nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament, and when historians compare them, "the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original" — with most of that remaining 0.5% being things like spelling variations, not changes in meaning. That same source notes complete Bibles exist dating back to 300 A.D., and comparing those to today's Bible shows they're essentially the same.

**Compared to other ancient texts, the Bible is unusually well-attested.** The Spanish EveryStudent source (cadaestudiante.com, "Libros de la Biblia - Historia de la Biblia") gives a helpful comparison: works like Plato's writings or Herodotus's Histories survive in only 5–20 copies, with gaps of 1,000+ years between the original and the oldest surviving copy. The New Testament has vastly more manuscripts and much smaller time gaps — which is exactly what scholars use to cross-check and reconstruct the original wording with confidence.

**On translation specifically**, the Vietnamese EveryStudent source makes an important clarification: translations aren't a game of "telephone" where each translation is based on the previous translation. Modern translations go back directly to the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic manuscripts (EveryVietStudent.com, "Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh").

So it's fair to say scribes made some copying errors over the centuries — that's just human reality. But it's not accurate to say we have "no idea" what the original said. Scholars can trace where and when changes happened precisely because there are so many manuscripts to compare (Sightline Ministry, "The Bible: How Big a Deal is Human Error?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

If you want, I'm happy to dig into a specific example your uncle might raise (like a particular "changed" verse, or the Dead Sea Scrolls comparison) — that can sometimes make this more concrete than general statistics.

Or it’s based on their experience with a single Christian. In view of that, here’s a short list of misconceptions that some have about Christians. They’re untrue. 1. Christians Disagree About Everything…Right? Definite misconception! Christians do not disagree about everything.

We agree that Jesus is the Son of God, and died on the cross and resurrected so that we could believe and be saved. We agree that God calls us to love our neighbor. We agree that humankind is inherently sinful without the grace of God, and that God loves us anyway. We agree that truth matters. We agree that the gospel of Jesus is Good News to this world. We agree that the Holy Spirit is with us, and that God has spoken truth to us through His words in Scripture. These core beliefs have carried on through the generations since Christianity first began.

That isn’t to say that things don’t get messy. We are, after all, human. There are plenty of theological disagreements to go around. But at the end of the day, most Christians recognize that the majority of disagreements needn’t divide us. We are still brothers and sisters, unified through Christ.

Our unity is accomplished through the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:3-4). Though we have disagreements, we are a family. That’s not to say there aren’t some strange uncles and wayward cousins.

2. Christians Are Opposed to Science…Right?

Definite misconception. Most Christians highly value the contributions of Science!

There are some Christians who take a strong obscurantist approach toward science, but I have not personally met one. Most of science doesn’t address things that concern faith in Christ. The speed of light, the chemistry of ammonium, the size of our sun, or the air speed velocity of an unladen swallow have little to do with the Gospel message. Yet for some reason, it remains a popular notion that Christians are hostile to science.

The Virgin Birth: Plausible, if God Exists

The Apostles’ Creed, an early creed of the Christian faith, affirms that Jesus Christ “was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.” If this belief is true, it means that Jesus’ entrance into human history isn’t just a tad different, but completely unique.

We can’t, of course, make the same kind of historical argument for the virgin birth that we can make for the resurrection. In the case of the resurrection, numerous eyewitnesses saw Jesus die and also later saw Him come back from the dead. But no eyewitness can attest to how Mary became pregnant. If Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that event was private.

Atheists declare it to be a “biological impossibility” for a virgin woman to give birth. In one sense they’re correct: humans, like other mammals, are normally incapable of parthenogenesis (a word that derives from Greek words meaning “virgin” and “birth”). But in another sense they’re completely wrong.

Affirming the virgin birth of Christ as “miraculous” does not mean having to believe that the laws of nature have been broken or violated. Just because a virgin birth is not naturally possible doesn’t mean we rule out the possibility of there being a God not bound by the laws of nature.

Is anything impossible for the God who designed and crafted our meticulously detailed universe?

The Virgin Birth: The Ultimate Miracle?

People in the ancient world knew that human conception naturally required sexual intercourse. For that reason, they viewed Jesus’ conception by Mary to be a miracle. Joseph, the man who took Mary as his wife, certainly believed that Mary was telling him the truth when she said she had yet to be with a man.

Writes the great Christian thinker C. S. Lewis,

Why Does God Allow Suffering?

by Faith Eng

“How can God be good when there is so much suffering in the world?”

This is a valid question. Christians believe that God is completely good and in ultimate control of our lives. How do we reconcile that idea with all the pain and suffering we see and experience?

There are answers to these questions, but not surprisingly, they can feel complex. Some experiences of suffering are on an individual, family or community level. Others are on a much larger scale.

There are many factors to consider, but the bottom line is: The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people.

The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life. To understand how this can be true, we’ll look at the overall story of God’s relationship with people in the Bible and where we are in that story now.

So if suffering is part of your reality right now, hopefully you will find fresh hope as you see God’s plan to end suffering once and for all.

Why Worship a God Who Allows Suffering?

Share this article

Q: "Why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?"

There probably is no greater violation than a child being raped. It’s devastating to the victim in so many ways. When coming to terms with it, rage is appropriate. There is no explanation for such actions.

However, it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it. It is not his fault that fathers molest their daughters or that mothers verbally abuse their sons.

We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose.

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent other people from doing evil to us?

How should we feel about the fact that God doesn't prevent us from doing evil to other people?

We might wish that God established a set of boundaries, beyond which people would be punished. We might suggest that God kill any man who molests a child.

Well then, how about the producers of child porn that might have helped motivate the man to molest the child? Would it be right if maybe God killed them too?

Ok, what should God do with, say, people who are verbally abusive? Words can wound deeply. It seems pretty apparent we get to do what we choose to do. And I don't see how we can be angry at God for letting us do that.

Hasn’t God revealed to us how to best live our lives?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 Commandments, no child would ever be raped or molested?

Is it not true that if everyone followed the 10 commandments, nothing would ever be stolen, no spouse would be betrayed, no one's son or daughter would be murdered?

Rather than control us, God gives us freedom. God does not interfere with anyone's choices. Rather he assures us that all will someday answer for what they have done and that justice will be administered. Judgment will be based on the guidelines given.

For all the evil that everyone of us from the beginning of our species has perpetrated, he paid the just penalty. None of us can comprehend that suffering. Though he was innocent, he voluntarily took upon himself the punishment that we deserve. And why? Because he loves us. It is like he is saying, “I know you don’t understand why I permit every evil. It’s not possible for you to understand yet. But just to show you that you can trust me, I’m going to suffer with you.”

I hear the weight in that question — it's not an abstract puzzle for you, it's a real objection, and honestly one of the hardest ones in all of human experience. Let me look for what grounded sources say, rather than offering you a tidy answer from my own head.I'm not going to pretend there's a clean, satisfying answer that makes the pain go away — because there isn't one, and I think you'd see right through it if I tried. What I found does wrestle with this honestly, though, without the dodge you're describing.

A few threads worth sitting with:

**God isn't the one causing it, but he does allow human freedom.** [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html) puts it bluntly when addressing this exact question about a child being harmed: "it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it." The argument is that for humans to be genuinely free — capable of real love, real choice — God doesn't override that freedom, even when people use it to devastate others. That's not a full answer to *why a child specifically*, but it's an honest attempt at the *why suffering exists at all* question.

**Some suffering isn't even about anyone's choices.** [Sightline Ministry](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this) points to the story of the man born blind, where Jesus's disciples assumed someone must have sinned to cause it — and Jesus said no, that's not why. The piece notes that some suffering comes from a broken world in general — disease, accidents, the physical laws of a fallen creation — not as punishment or a lesson, just as a reality of "sin in the world" that harms the innocent along with everyone else.

**Christianity doesn't claim suffering proves God's absence — it points to something else entirely.** [Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html) argues that "suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people," and that God "ultimately does not want people to suffer" even though it's real in this life now.

**And this is the part I think matters most for a question like yours:** [thelife](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3) makes the point that "a child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance." Their answer isn't a theory — it's that God, in Jesus, didn't stay distant from suffering but entered it: "He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form... he SUFFERED." The claim there is that God's response to the problem isn't an argument, it's presence — Jesus taking on suffering himself rather than explaining it away from a safe distance.

I want to be honest with you: none of that erases the horror of a child actually suffering right now, today. If you're carrying something specific — your own pain, or someone else's — I'd rather sit with that than hand you philosophy. What's underneath the question for you?

happened after a game of chess. “Daddy, do you know where you’ll spend eternity when you die?” I asked him. “Well, I hope I’ll go to heaven, baby,” he replied. “Can I share with you how you can be sure?”

When my dad first told me that he was not afraid to die, that he was ready to go whenever God saw fit to take him, I didn’t know what to say. I was uncomfortable with the idea of Dad dying, though I was happy for him to be at peace about it. This was probably about 5 to 10 years ago. When he did pass this last January, he told my mom he was ready to go and meet Jesus. He was 90 years old, and his body was worn out. My youngest daughter joked that God knew better than to argue with Grandpa!

When I led a small family graveside gathering in July, I focused on a Scripture that Dad often quoted from 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 which he summarized simply as “absent from the body, present with the Lord.”

So here is what we can always be certain about. As long as we are at home in our bodies, we are away from the Lord. We live by believing, not by seeing. We are certain about that. We would rather be away from our bodies and at home with the Lord. So we try our best to please him. We want to please him whether we are at home in our bodies or away from them.

My brother, who has terminal cancer, has often heard my dad talk about death in this way, so when I visited my brother, who is in hospice, I found that I was quoting Dad when my brother was grieving the loss of the close relationship he and my dad had, reminding my brother of what he had often heard Dad say. This thought also gives my brother peace about his own impending death.

The most frightening thing about death is that we are not in control. We did not choose to be born, and we do not have much choice about when we will die. Death is really an “unknown” to us except when we watch those close to us pass from this life.

My father’s suicide catapulted me into a time of deep grief, a time when I questioned all I thought I knew about God while clinging to him daily for the strength to get through the pain. In those first shock-filled days after I heard the news that my father had hung himself in the basement of our home, my heart would scream: “NO, NO, don’t think about it! It hurts too much!”

After the funeral, when I left to return to university, I felt so alone and overwhelmed. Whenever I had time to think, I would think of Dad and cry.

Questions and doubts started to fill my mind:

If God loved me, why had he allowed this disaster?

If God was all-powerful, why hadn’t he stopped my dad?

If God was all-knowing, why didn’t he let me know how despairing my father was? Why hadn’t he shown me how to reach him?

If God was there, why hadn’t he done something?

Was God there?

I had become a Christian a few years earlier. The thought that Jesus had died for me so I could be forgiven and enter into a personal relationship with him had filled me with surprise. I could know God? He could be closer to me than a brother? Of course I wanted to know him! Of course I wanted to be forgiven! And when, at 16, I invited him to come into my life and forgive me and change me, he had done so, filling my heart with a sense of his presence.

But now, for the first time, God had really disappointed me. And I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too. You see, my father and I had spent time together just a few days before he died, and he had asked me questions about God I couldn’t answer. Then he had asked me to transfer back to the university at home so I could be near him and I had refused to do so. Now, I wondered if he would still be alive if I had done what he wanted, and I was tormented by a deep sense of guilt.

God had really disappointed me. I felt that I had deeply disappointed him, too.

Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

by Matt Perman

The doctrine of the Trinity is foundational to the Christian faith. It is crucial for properly understanding what God is like, how He relates to us, and how we should relate to Him.

But it also raises many difficult questions. How can God be both one and three? Is the Trinity a contradiction? If Jesus is God, why do the Gospels record instances where He prayed to God?

While we cannot fully understand everything about the Trinity (or anything else), it is possible to answer questions like these and come to a solid grasp of what it means for God to be three in one.

Use the links below to jump to a specific section:

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

Is the Trinity Contradictory?

Essence and Person

Trinitarian Illustrations?

Summary

Application

What Does it Mean That God is a Trinity?

The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person. These definitions express three crucial truths: (1) The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each Person is fully God, (3) there is only one God.

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons

The Bible speaks of the Father as God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus as God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Are these just three different ways of looking at God, or simply ways of referring to three different roles that God plays?

The answer must be no, because the Bible also indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons. For example, since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son. Likewise, after the Son returned to the Father (John 16:10), the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). Therefore, the Holy Spirit must be distinct from the Father and the Son.
sources.title: Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief

Dreieinigkeit - was ist das?

Artikel anhören

Frage: „Was kann ich mir unter der Dreieinigkeit vorstellen? Was bedeutet sie?“

Der Begriff „Dreieinigkeit“ oder „Dreifaltigkeit“ findet sich so nicht in der Bibel, aber er fasst gut zusammen, was sie über Gott aussagt. In der Bibel wird uns Gott vorgestellt als der Vater, der Sohn und der Heilige Geist. Gleichzeitig wird immer wieder betont, dass es nur einen Gott gibt. Die Bezeichnung „Dreieinigkeit“ trifft also den Nagel auf den Kopf! Sie drückt aus, was die Bibel uns über Gott offenbart: Dass er in drei Personen präsent ist, die doch das gleiche göttliche Wesen darstellen.

Es gibt ein paar interessante Versuche, diese Dreieinigkeit zu veranschaulichen. Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Wasser (H2O): Es existiert in verschiedenen Aggregatzuständen, nämlich als Wasser, Eis oder Dampf. Die Erscheinungsformen sind sehr verschieden, aber das Wesen ist das Gleiche: H2O. Ein anderer Vergleich ist die Wärme: Sie kann in Form von Strahlung auftreten, als Wärmestrom oder auch in festen Körpern geleitet werden.

Der Sohn (Jesus) ist ganz Gott. Der Vater ist ganz Gott. Und der Heilige Geist ist völlig ganz Gott. Trotzdem gibt es nur einen Gott. Mit unserem begrenzten Horizont ist das schwer zu begreifen. Aber schon ganz am Anfang wird Gott so beschrieben! Achtet mal auf die Pronomen im Plural schon im Schöpfungsbericht: „Und Gott sprach: Lasst uns Menschen machen nach unserem Bilde …“1

Ein paar weitere Bibelstellen, die das „Puzzle der Dreieinigkeit“ zusammensetzen:

Es gibt nur einen Gott:

„Höre, Israel! Der HERR ist unser Gott, der HERR allein (einzig).“2

„Ich bin der HERR, und es gibt keinen außer mir.“3

„Es gibt keinen Gott außer dem einen.“4

Jesus ist Gott, eins mit dem Vater:

Jesus sagte: „Ich und der Vater sind eins.“5

„Wer mich sieht, sieht den Vater.“6

„Wer an mich glaubt, glaubt an den, der mich gesandt hat.“7

Der Heilige Geist:

„Wenn jemand nicht den Geist Christi hat, gehört er nicht zu ihm.“8

That's a really fair question — and one Christians themselves have wrestled with for centuries. Let me lay out what's actually being claimed, because the key is that it's not saying God is three *and* one in the *same sense*.

**The core claim**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," the doctrine means there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It breaks down into three things held together: (1) the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each is fully God, and (3) there is only one God ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

**Why it's not a contradiction**

The resolution lies in a distinction between two different words: *essence* and *person*. God is one in *essence* (what he is — his being, his "substance") but three in *person* (who he is — distinct relational identities). A contradiction would only occur if Christians said God is three in the *same* way he is one — but that's not the claim. As the Spanish-language version of that same Cru article puts it, "Solo habría una contradicción si decimos que Dios es tres en la misma forma que él es uno" ("There would only be a contradiction if we said God is three in the same way he is one") — [Cru](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

EveryStudent.com offers a simple way to picture this with math: it's not 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1 — hence the word "Trinity" (Tri = three, Unity = one) ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

**Why the Bible pushes Christians to say this**

- The Father is called God (Phil. 1:2), the Son is called God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit is called God (Acts 5:3-4) — Cru points out this rules out saying they're just three names or roles for the same one thing.
- Yet they're shown as distinct: the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), the Son returns to the Father and they send the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33) — so they can't just be the same person wearing different masks ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).
- At the same time, Scripture insists firmly there's only one God — "Höre, Israel! Der HERR ist unser Gott, der HERR allein" (Deut. 6:4) and "Ich bin der HERR, und es gibt keinen außer mir" — cited in the German EveryStudent article ([EveryStudent — German](https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html)).

**On the illustrations**

People have tried analogies — water existing as ice, liquid, and steam; or the sun giving light, heat, and radiation — but as EveryStudent notes plainly, "No illustration is going to be perfect" ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)). It's genuinely a mystery — one article calls it "perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith" ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)).

So the honest Christian answer isn't "we've fully solved this puzzle" — it's "we believe this is what Scripture reveals about God, even though it stretches our categories, because God isn't bound by the limits we are." Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense, or would it help to dig into why Christians think the Bible pushes them toward this conclusion in the first place?

A related point of difference is the crucifixion and resurrection — Muslims generally do not believe Jesus died on the cross, while for Christians, his death and resurrection are foundational truths of the faith (same source).

**On the meaning of "Son of God."** Islam strongly rejects the idea that God could have a son, seeing it as incompatible with belief in one indivisible God. Christianity, though, doesn't understand Jesus's sonship in a physical or biological sense. As EveryStudent.sk explains, Christians understand "Jesus's sonship not in a bodily sense, but in a spiritual sense. Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical union of a man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit" (EveryStudent.sk, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)). That source also notes that the prophet Isaiah, long before Jesus's birth, described a coming child as "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" — which Christians see as pointing forward to Jesus.

**Why Christians see Jesus as the fulfillment, not just another prophet in a line.** Islam holds that God revealed his message progressively through various prophets, with Muhammad as the last one. The Christian view, according to that same EveryStudent.sk piece, is different: "God does not change his plan. From the beginning he sent prophets to bring people back into relationship with him... Christianity does not see its faith as one stage to be replaced by another, but as the fulfillment of what God promised from the beginning" — pointing to Jesus's own words, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. One of the most important features of Christian faith is accepting that Jesus is God. Christians are in trouble, then, if Jesus never made such a claim of himself! Yet many have argued that this is exactly the case: Jesus never claimed to be God, they say, and his divinity is an invention of the Christian church. Is this true?

I have found that there are two main reasons why people think Jesus never claimed to be God. Let’s take a look!

Jesus never said the exact phrase, “I am God”

Some people believe Jesus never claimed to be God because, in reading the Gospels of Jesus, they simply don’t see Jesus saying “I am God” (or something along those lines). While it’s true that the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, “I am God,” the Gospels still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God. Examples include “The Father and I are one” (John 10:30) and “Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). I work through many more verses In one of my early YouTube videos, “Did Jesus really Say He was God?” While it’s always possible to reinterpret or raise skepticism over the meaning of any statement, the most natural and common-sense understanding of these quotations is that Jesus is claiming to be God.

Related: Do We “Get” Jesus?

The Gospel of John is not reliable

The second reason given to deny Jesus’s claim to divinity is this: to challenge the historical reliability of the Gospel of John. It’s well understood that John has the clearest examples of Jesus claiming to be God, and it was (probably) also the latest of the four Gospels written. So, many conclude that Jesus never claimed to be God, yet legend developed over time that he did. The earliest Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—did not include this legend because not enough time had passed. But John, which came later, has the legendary stuff. Notice how this argument admits that John presents Jesus as God, but it denies that John is a good source to use.

More Than a Carpenter blog #whoisjesus

Welcome! In this post we’ll dive into whether Jesus claimed to be God.

Did Jesus claim to be just a great spiritual guide — or God in human form?

Jesus Humbly Claimed His Deity

Some skeptics like to assert that Jesus wasn’t God — and never claimed to be. We should scratch our heads in confusion at these claims, because the Bible’s New Testament writers clearly wrote otherwise.

John records that Jesus said, without ego, “Most assuredly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I AM.” At this claim of deity, the Jewish crowd grabbed stones to kill Him. Why? Because they knew that, according to Mosaic law, any person daring to make such a claim was deserving of death. They understood Jesus to be claiming that He was God.

When the high priest later asked Jesus, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus replied, “I am. That's a fair and important question — and it's worth being honest about the nuance here.

**The direct answer: Jesus never says the exact English sentence "I am God."** But there's one moment where his words in the original context carry that exact weight, without needing anyone's interpretation to get there.

**John 8:58** — Jesus says: *"Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!"* (as quoted by Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god and https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false)

That phrase "I am" isn't just a grammatical oddity — it's the same phrase God uses to name himself to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14 ("I AM WHO I AM"). Jesus takes that divine name and applies it to himself. The reaction of the people listening confirms they heard it that way too: according to Sightline Ministry, they immediately picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy — the punishment under Jewish law for claiming to be God (https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false).

A second strong instance, at his trial: In **Mark 14:61-63**, the high priest asks Jesus directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers simply, **"I am."** The high priest tears his robes and cries "Blasphemy!" — again, the listeners themselves understood this as a claim to deity (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html; Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false).

There's also **John 10:30** — *"The Father and I are one"* — which led the Jewish leaders present to say back to him, "You, a mere man, claim to be God" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html). That's not a later theologian's spin — that's how the people standing right there in the room reacted to his own words.

So to be candid with you: Jesus's approach was less "I hereby declare I am God" and more using language, titles, and claims (like taking God's own name, or saying "I and the Father are one") that his Jewish audience — who knew their scriptures intimately — immediately recognized as a claim to divinity. That's why I've quoted the actual sentences and also told you how the original hearers reacted, so you can weigh it yourself rather than take anyone's word for what it means.

Would you like to dig into the context of John 8:58 more, or look at how the Gospel writers themselves describe who they believed Jesus to be?

To declare that the Bible has been “altered” over the centuries could mean a number of different things.

For instance, you could talk about how later scribes added punctuation markings, lower-case lettering, etc., as their Greek language evolved over time. But that is of little concern. When most people say that the Bible has been altered, they mean that the original written text has changed in content over many years, is now corrupted, and the original meaning lost.

It is very common these days to hear someone say that the Bible has been altered. This might come from a skeptic, but it also might come from followers of other religions that have spun off the Christian tradition such as Mormonism, Jehovah’s Witnesses, or Islam. In asserting that the biblical text became corrupted, they add that their religion’s holy writings have corrected the problem. And they use their holy writings to provide new spiritual insights that support their religious view.

Understanding the term “altered”

Despite certain anti-Christian motivations to challenge the Bible, we don’t have compelling reasons to believe that the modern Bible is wildly different from what was originally written. Even though we don’t have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts.

These manuscripts have some differences, and this is to be expected because of human error. But there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy. We can see what was altered.

But what if the original text was changed before a bunch of copies were made? If this happened, then all of our copies would have come from a bad text, and we would never be able to know what was originally written!

Also, you might be familiar with the more recent archeological findings of the Dead Sea Scrolls. These were found in the caves of Qumran, just off the northwest corner of the Dead Sea.

Researchers have compared the Bible we have today with what they found, and they remained highly similar, nearly 100% identical.

Don't let anyone tell you that the New Testament or the Bible has been changed from its original writing. That simply is not historically accurate.

The Bible has not been changed.

Your uncle is raising a fair question — it's one scholars have actually studied carefully, and there's good reason to think his conclusion (that we *can't* know) is too pessimistic. Here's what the evidence shows:

**We don't have the originals, but we have a LOT of copies.** According to Sightline Ministry, "we don't have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries). For the New Testament specifically, there are nearly 25,000 hand-written manuscript copies of portions of it (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**The copies overwhelmingly agree with each other.** Historians who've compared these thousands of manuscripts have concluded the New Testament we have today is "at least 99.5% accurate to the original," with the small remaining differences being things like spelling variations rather than changes in meaning (EveryStudent, same source above).

**How this compares to other ancient texts.** A helpful comparison from EveryStudent — Spanish shows that for classical works like Plato, Herodotus, or Tacitus, we typically have far fewer surviving manuscripts (5–20) and a much longer gap between the original and the earliest copy (1,000+ years) — yet historians don't doubt those texts are reliably reconstructed. The Bible has vastly more manuscript evidence and closer time gaps (https://www.cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html).

**Scholars can actually trace the changes.** Sightline Ministry notes that because there are so many manuscripts to cross-check, "scholars can identify the original reading with a high degree of confidence... scholars can clearly see the path of where and when mistakes and changes were made" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

**Ancient copies confirm this too.** The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls (much older Old Testament manuscripts) allowed researchers to compare them with later Bibles — they were found to be "nearly 100% identical" (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

So it's not that the Bible was copied so many times that we lost track — it's more that having *so many* copies actually lets scholars cross-check and reconstruct the original text with a high degree of confidence. That said, it's a topic worth digging into more if you or your uncle are curious — there's real scholarship behind this, not just faith claims. Is there a particular part of this — like translation methods, or specific "changes" people point to — you'd like to explore further?

Or it’s based on their experience with a single Christian. In view of that, here’s a short list of misconceptions that some have about Christians. They’re untrue. 1. Christians Disagree About Everything…Right? Definite misconception! Christians do not disagree about everything.

We agree that Jesus is the Son of God, and died on the cross and resurrected so that we could believe and be saved. We agree that God calls us to love our neighbor. We agree that humankind is inherently sinful without the grace of God, and that God loves us anyway. We agree that truth matters. We agree that the gospel of Jesus is Good News to this world. We agree that the Holy Spirit is with us, and that God has spoken truth to us through His words in Scripture. These core beliefs have carried on through the generations since Christianity first began.

That isn’t to say that things don’t get messy. We are, after all, human. There are plenty of theological disagreements to go around. But at the end of the day, most Christians recognize that the majority of disagreements needn’t divide us. We are still brothers and sisters, unified through Christ.

Our unity is accomplished through the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13, Ephesians 4:3-4). Though we have disagreements, we are a family. That’s not to say there aren’t some strange uncles and wayward cousins.

2. Christians Are Opposed to Science…Right?

Definite misconception. Most Christians highly value the contributions of Science!

There are some Christians who take a strong obscurantist approach toward science, but I have not personally met one. Most of science doesn’t address things that concern faith in Christ. The speed of light, the chemistry of ammonium, the size of our sun, or the air speed velocity of an unladen swallow have little to do with the Gospel message. Yet for some reason, it remains a popular notion that Christians are hostile to science.
sources.title: Five Misconceptions of Christians

The Virgin Birth: Plausible, if God Exists

The Apostles’ Creed, an early creed of the Christian faith, affirms that Jesus Christ “was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary.” If this belief is true, it means that Jesus’ entrance into human history isn’t just a tad different, but completely unique.

We can’t, of course, make the same kind of historical argument for the virgin birth that we can make for the resurrection. In the case of the resurrection, numerous eyewitnesses saw Jesus die and also later saw Him come back from the dead. But no eyewitness can attest to how Mary became pregnant. If Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, that event was private.

Atheists declare it to be a “biological impossibility” for a virgin woman to give birth. In one sense they’re correct: humans, like other mammals, are normally incapable of parthenogenesis (a word that derives from Greek words meaning “virgin” and “birth”). But in another sense they’re completely wrong.

Affirming the virgin birth of Christ as “miraculous” does not mean having to believe that the laws of nature have been broken or violated. Just because a virgin birth is not naturally possible doesn’t mean we rule out the possibility of there being a God not bound by the laws of nature.

Is anything impossible for the God who designed and crafted our meticulously detailed universe?

The Virgin Birth: The Ultimate Miracle?

People in the ancient world knew that human conception naturally required sexual intercourse. For that reason, they viewed Jesus’ conception by Mary to be a miracle. Joseph, the man who took Mary as his wife, certainly believed that Mary was telling him the truth when she said she had yet to be with a man.

Writes the great Christian thinker C. S. Lewis,
